column3: Falling blocks. A 64x192 tower is a real falling-block well (about 10 columns of 6 px cells, the classic proportions), with bevelled, glossy tetromino cells in a designed palette, a ghost piece and a little 'NEXT' window. The time is stacked in the well: an AI player drops pieces so that the settled stack spells the digits (hours above minutes, or a design of your own), letterforms built from tetromino cells (design a cell font that is buildable from the seven pieces). Always alive: a piece is always falling, rotating and sliding with smooth sub-cell motion; the player tucks pieces in with T-spins. Minute turn: the changing digit's rows are completed and cleared (the classic flash, collapse with gravity, never showing a different number), then new pieces rain in to build the new digit. Hour: a TETRIS: four-line clear, the well flashes, the level counter goes up and the colour scheme changes. Hypnotic, smooth, satisfying.

Plasma globe. A glass sphere with a glowing electrode at its centre fills the panel: violet-pink plasma filaments writhe out from the core to the glass (real-looking: branching, flickering, drifting, each filament a soft glowing ribbon with a hot white core). The time is where the filaments land: a fingertip-shaped contact pattern on the glass, so the filaments reach out and touch the glass along the strokes of the numerals (filament-script digits: brighter, denser filament bundles forming the strokes, the rest of the globe a living web). Always alive: filaments crawl and crackle, the core pulses, the glass has a rim highlight and reflections. Minute turn: the changing digit's filaments let go one by one and snap to the new digit's strokes (electric, smooth, physical). Hour: a hand touches the globe, every filament rushes to the palm, a discharge flash, then they redistribute into the time. Electric light on black GOB.

Orrery. A 128x128 brass mechanical orrery in real 3D (slightly tilted view, perspective), with arms, gears and a glowing sun at the centre. Not digits: the time is read from the planets' positions against a ring of engraved hour markers on the brass rim, like the urwerk and ressence watches the owner loved. Design a clear system: e.g. a big planet orbits once in 12 hours (hour), its moon orbits once an hour (minute), a tiny comet or moonlet sweeps the seconds; or the planets arranged so the hour planet's ring carries engraved minute numerals. It must read from 2 m. Always alive: everything orbits smoothly, the sun's corona flickers, planets show day/night shading from the sun, the brass gleams with moving specular highlights. Minute turn: a gentle tick of the gear train and a numeral lights. Hour: an eclipse, or all planets align and a chime ring passes through the arms. Elegant, 3D, constantly dynamic.

Cuckoo clock. A 64x128 carved Black Forest cuckoo clock: a chalet roof with carved leaves and a bird on top, a little door, a dial or carved numeral plaques, and below it the long pendulum and two pinecone weights on chains (the tall layout is the clock's own shape). The owner's rainbow frog in round glasses is the 'cuckoo' (bold, simple design, 16+ px when it is out). The time is shown by the clock itself, in carved-wood letterforms on the plaques or an ornate dial designed for this grid. Always alive: the pendulum swings with real physics, the escapement ticks, the weights creep down the chains over the hour, a little waterwheel turns or dancers rotate on a turntable. Minute turn: the plaque flips or a carved wheel rotates to the new numeral. Hour: the door bursts open and the frog pops out and croaks the hour count, the dancers spin, and a hand winds the weights back up. Charm, wood, warm lamplight.

Conveyor sushi. A 256x64 kaiten-zushi counter seen from the side or slightly above: a conveyor belt runs the whole banner length, carrying plates of sushi (nigiri, maki, tamago, ikura, a little soy dish) with a sushi chef behind the counter. The time is made of sushi: maki rolls and nigiri arranged on four long plates into numerals, or the digits drawn on plates in sauce, or (better) the numerals ARE sushi pieces (design sushi letterforms: a 0 is a maki roll, a 1 a nigiri on its side, nori bands, rice grains, fish sheen). The belt moves constantly and smoothly. Minute turn: the plate with the changing digit rides off the end of the banner and the chef plates a new one (knife flashes, pieces placed), which slides into its spot. Hour: a bullet-train sushi delivery zooms the whole length with a special platter, steam, the chef bows. Food glossiness and the belt motion are the point; the owner's frog can be a customer grabbing plates.

Pin art. A 128x128 pin-art toy (the pinscreen desk toy): a field of thousands of polished metal pins seen head-on in a frame, lit by a low raking light so each pin head is a little sphere with a highlight and each pushed-out pin casts a shadow and shows its shaft. The time is pressed into the pins from behind as relief: big raised numerals of pins (design relief letterforms: rounded, like a hand or object pressed in). Always alive: a slow wave ripples through the pins, the light drifts round, pins settle with tiny bounces. Minute turn: the changing digit is pushed back flat by a sweeping hand from the front (pins sliding back in a wave) and the new one is pressed out from behind by an object shaped like the numeral (pins rising in sequence with real spring motion). Hour: the whole field is pushed out by a hand (the owner's frog face pressed into the pins for a moment, recognisable), then the time is pressed again. Physical, metallic, hypnotic like zensand.

Space invaders. A 128x64 arcade invader game: the invader formation IS the time: four big digits built of small animated aliens (two-frame marching animation, three alien species with designed sprites), marching side to side and stepping down as one formation with the classic accelerating heartbeat. The defender is the owner's rainbow frog in round glasses in a little tank (bold, simple sprite, 10+ px), with shields at the bottom that erode. A UFO crosses now and then. Always alive at 60 fps: smooth sub-pixel motion for the frog and shots, the formation stepping on the beat. Minute turn: the frog shoots the changing digit's aliens one by one (pixel explosions), and a new wave of aliens drops in from the top and lines up as the new digit (never a different number on the way). Hour: the mothership descends, a big boss fight, then the formation returns. A game the owner would watch.

Knitted sweater. The panel is a close-up of a hand-knitted Fair Isle sweater: real knit stitches (each stitch a little V of yarn with fuzz and shading, about 3-4 px), in a warm wool palette. The time is knitted into the colourwork: numerals in stranded-knit letterforms designed on the stitch grid (big, bold, with the slight stitch-shape distortion of real knitting). Always alive: two knitting needles at the top knit the next row across the panel with a clicking rhythm, the yarn from two balls (rolling a little, the frog or a kitten batting one) feeds in, the fabric breathes and sways. Minute turn: the changing digit is unravelled (the yarn pulls out stitch by stitch in a wavy kinked strand) and re-knitted row by row with the needles. Hour: the whole sweater scrolls up as a new band of pattern (a frog motif, snowflakes) is knitted. Cosy, tactile, alive.

Neon alley. Three panels in an L: the tall arm is a rainy night street canyon of buildings with vertical neon signs (Tokyo / Hong Kong style), the long bottom arm is the wet street and its puddles. The time is the signage: big vertical neon signs whose characters are the digits (design several neon sign letterforms: tube neon with real glass-tube glow, a blinking broken tube, a buzzing flicker; plus a lit box sign or a hologram), and every sign is reflected in the puddles below with ripples from the rain. Always alive: rain streaks (slanted, sub-pixel), drips from awnings, steam from a vent, a cat or the rainbow frog under an umbrella walking the street, a passing car's headlights sweeping. Minute turn: the changing sign flickers out tube by tube with a buzz and a dying-tube stutter, and the new numeral strikes on segment by segment, warming up from orange to full colour. Hour: a train passes on an elevated track with lit windows, the whole street flickers, signs re-ignite in a wave. Moody, cinematic.

Stained-glass window. Five panels in a plus are a cross-shaped cathedral window: deep jewel-coloured glass panes (ruby, cobalt, emerald, amber) held by dark lead came, with painted detail and glass texture (streaks, bubbles, uneven colour density). The time is in the glass itself: numerals leaded into the design (gothic or art-nouveau letterforms designed as came-and-glass, one per arm, the centre a rose medallion with a seconds motif). The light behind it is the sky and follows the real time of day: the sun moves behind the window, so panes glow brighter or dimmer, God rays and floating dust in front, clouds passing make the whole window breathe; at night, candlelight from inside, faint moonlight. Minute turn: the changing digit's panes go dark as a cloud-shadow sweeps over them, and the new numeral's panes catch the light pane by pane (as if a glazier relit them). Hour: the bells: the rose spins its pattern, light floods every pane and the hour panes flash. Use the cross shape.

Robot factory. A 192x64 automated workshop: two industrial robot arms (real inverse kinematics, three joints, smooth eased motion, hydraulic shading, warning stripes) work at a bench under a hanging lamp. The digits are machined parts: big steel or aluminium numerals cut from plate, with bevelled edges and specular highlights (machined letterforms: chamfered, with bolt holes), standing in jigs. Always alive: the arms idle, polish, inspect with a scanning laser, a conveyor carries bolts, sparks or chips fly, status LEDs blink. Minute turn: one arm lifts the changing digit out of its jig and drops it in a bin, the other arm welds or cuts the new numeral from a plate (welding sparks, a glowing seam cooling from white to orange to steel) and places it. Hour: both arms do a synchronised flourish, a forklift with the owner's frog drives through, or the parts are spray-painted a new colour. Mechanical choreography is the wow.

Sand pour. A 64x128 glass vessel of falling-sand physics (cellular automaton grains, each a pixel with warm sand colours and strata: amber, rust, cream, a little black): sand pours from a funnel at the top through baffles and settles into piles. The time is moulded in sand: digit-shaped hollow moulds (glass outlines) fill with sand, or the sand settles into numerals held between invisible walls (design letterforms for poured sand: rounded tops of the piles, the angle of repose, strata). Always alive: a thin stream always falls, grains bounce and slide, the pile surface avalanches. Minute turn: a trapdoor under the changing digit opens, its sand drains away through the vessel (a beautiful cascade) and the mould refills from the funnel (partly filled must never read as another number). Hour: the whole vessel inverts (rotates 180 deg smoothly, like an hourglass) and all the sand flows back through the baffles, then the time is poured again. Deterministic: derive state from the minute, warmup <= 2 s. The owner loved sand.
